tts: You've probably seen them: running shoes with strange hollow pods on the bottom, like little clouds. They're made by a Swiss company called On. Last year, On sold more than three billion Swiss francs' worth of shoes and clothing, and its sales grew by thirty percent, while Nike's revenue went down. And here's the crazy part: the whole thing started with a man cutting up a garden hose in his kitchen. To understand why that idea was so powerful, we need to go back almost two hundred years, to the moment rubber stopped being useless. This is the story of the sneaker.

In the early eighteen hundreds, natural rubber was a disaster. People made raincoats and boots out of it, but in summer it melted into a sticky, smelly mess, and in winter it cracked like glass. Then an American inventor named Charles Goodyear became obsessed with fixing it. He went broke, he went to debtors' prison, and he kept experimenting. In eighteen thirty-nine, the legend says, he dropped a mix of rubber and sulfur onto a hot stove, and instead of melting, it turned firm and flexible. That process is called vulcanization. Goodyear patented it, but spent years fighting copycats and died deeply in debt. The tire company that carries his name was founded decades later, by people who had nothing to do with him.

Vulcanized rubber could finally be glued to canvas. In Britain, these cheap canvas shoes were called plimsolls. In America, people noticed something else: the rubber soles were silent. You could walk right up behind someone without a sound. You could sneak. And by the eighteen-eighties, people were calling them sneakers. In nineteen sixteen, the U.S. Rubber Company launched Keds, one of the first mass-market sneaker brands. Around the same time, Converse released the All Star basketball shoe. In the twenties, a salesman and former player named Chuck Taylor drove across America, running basketball clinics and selling shoes. It worked so well that his name went onto the ankle patch, and it's still there today.

Now let's go to a small town in Germany called Herzogenaurach. In nineteen twenty-four, Adi Dassler started making sports shoes in his mother's laundry room. His older brother Rudolf joined him, and their shoes were good. At the nineteen thirty-six Berlin Olympics, Jesse Owens won four gold medals wearing Dassler spikes. But the brothers didn't get along. After the war, they split for good. In nineteen forty-eight, Rudolf started his own company, which became Puma. A year later, Adi registered Adidas. The two factories sat on opposite sides of the same small river, and the town split with them. Locals were said to look down at your shoes before deciding whether to talk to you.

Across the ocean, a track coach named Bill Bowerman and one of his former runners, Phil Knight, started a small business importing Japanese running shoes. In nineteen seventy-one, they launched their own brand: Nike. The swoosh logo was designed by a student, Carolyn Davidson, for thirty-five dollars. That same year, Bowerman wanted a sole that would grip a new synthetic track. So he poured urethane into his wife's waffle iron, ruining it completely. But the waffle pattern worked, and it became one of Nike's first hit shoes. Then, in nineteen eighty-five, Nike signed a rookie named Michael Jordan. The Air Jordan line reportedly brought in over a hundred million dollars in its first year, and sneakers became culture.

In the nineteen-seventies, jogging exploded in America, and suddenly millions of ordinary people needed running shoes. From then on, the big brands fought an arms race over cushioning: air bubbles, gels, softer and softer foams. Running shoes got bigger and more padded, but many runners still complained about the same thing. A soft shoe feels great when you land, but it can feel mushy when you push off. Olivier Bernhard knew this feeling well. He was a Swiss professional triathlete and Ironman winner, and he struggled with injuries. After retiring, he wanted a shoe that was soft on landing and firm on take-off at the same time. In the late two-thousands, he worked with a Swiss engineer and tried something absurd: he cut a garden hose into short pieces and glued them sideways onto the bottom of a running shoe.

It looked ridiculous, but it worked. When your foot lands, each hollow piece squashes, both down and back, and absorbs the impact. Then, once it's fully compressed, it becomes firm, and you push off against something solid. Inside the sole there's also a stiff plate, called the Speedboard, that flexes like a spring and helps you roll forward. Bernhard reportedly showed the idea to big brands, and they weren't interested. So, in twenty ten, he started his own company in Zurich, together with two friends, David Allemann and Caspar Coppetti. They called it On. That same year, their prototype won an award at ISPO, one of the biggest sporting goods trade shows in the world. The garden hose pieces were redesigned into engineered rubber pods, and patented as CloudTec.

For years, On grew quietly, through specialty running stores and word of mouth. Then came the moment that changed everything. In twenty nineteen, after his long contract with Nike ended, Roger Federer didn't sign a normal sponsorship deal. He invested in On and became a partner, helping design shoes, including a line called The Roger. Two years later, in September twenty twenty-one, On went public on the New York Stock Exchange. The shares were priced at twenty-four dollars, opened above thirty-five, and the company was valued at more than eleven billion dollars on its first day. In twenty twenty-four, actress Zendaya joined as a partner too. A running shoe from Zurich had become a fashion statement.

Now look at the numbers. In twenty twenty-one, On's sales were about seven hundred million Swiss francs. In twenty twenty-two, one point two billion. Then one point eight. Then two point three. And in twenty twenty-five, just over three billion, up thirty percent in a single year. On keeps almost sixty-three cents of gross profit from every franc of sales, which is very high for a shoe company. For comparison, Nike is still more than ten times bigger, but On is growing much faster. Sales in the Asia-Pacific region nearly doubled, to more than half a billion francs. The secret is a mix of things: a product that looks different, prices that stay high, very few discounts, and a story that's easy to tell. And that story is still a piece of garden hose.

So, look at the whole journey. A broke inventor and a hot stove gave us rubber that doesn't melt. Silent soles gave us the word sneaker. Two feuding brothers gave us Adidas and Puma. A waffle iron helped build Nike. And a retired triathlete with a garden hose built a company worth billions. Every big jump in sneaker history came from someone who looked at an ordinary material and asked: what if? One of the most famous soles in history came out of a waffle iron, and one of the fastest-growing shoe brands came out of a garden hose. Maybe the next one is sitting in your kitchen right now.
